#| label: setup

library(tidymodels)

## The assumption behind every standard error

Nearly every method in this course assumes that one row tells you nothing about the next. That
assumption is what turns *n* rows into *n* pieces of evidence: it is the reason standard errors
shrink with $\sqrt{n}$, the reason cross-validation works, and the reason a *p*-value means
anything.

Marine data violates it routinely, and usually by design. You revisit the same monitoring
stations. You take three sub-samples from one grab. You measure twenty individuals from one
haul. You record a CTD profile every metre. In each case the number of rows in your spreadsheet
is much larger than the number of independent things you learned.

This page measures the gap on the coastal survey and shows what it does to a result you might
otherwise have published.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

## The idea

### Pseudo-replication

Treating repeated measurements of the same unit as independent replicates is called
**pseudo-replication**. It does not usually bias your estimates; what it does is make them look
far more certain than they are.

The mechanism is simple. Two visits to the same site share everything the site has that your
covariates do not measure: a rock ledge, a persistent eddy, a patch of the population. When the
model is wrong at that site, it tends to be wrong in the same direction on both visits. Those
two errors are not two independent pieces of evidence about the model; they are closer to one.

Common marine cases, all of which look like independent rows:

| What is repeated | What the rows share | The unit you actually have |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Annual visits to fixed stations | Local habitat, depth, substrate | The station |
| Sub-samples from one grab or core | The grab | The grab |
| Individuals measured from one haul | The haul, the gear, the day | The haul |
| Points along a CTD profile | The cast, the water column | The cast |
| Images from one transect | Illumination, habitat patch | The transect |

### Measuring it

The **intra-class correlation** (ICC) is the proportion of the total variation that sits
*between* groups rather than within them. Zero means the grouping tells you nothing; one means
everything within a group is identical.

From it comes the number that matters, the **design effect**:

$$\text{design effect} = 1 + (\bar{m} - 1)\,\rho, \qquad n_{\text{eff}} = \frac{n}{\text{design effect}}$$

where $\rho$ is the ICC and $\bar{m}$ is the average group size. The effective sample size
$n_{\text{eff}}$ is roughly how many genuinely independent observations your rows are worth.

## Worked example

The raw survey export carries `site_id`: the 720 usable visits come from a smaller number of
repeatedly visited monitoring sites.

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

d <- survey |>
  select(site_id, abundance, depth_m, temperature_c, chlorophyll_mg_m3,
         salinity_psu, substrate, season) |>
  drop_na()

visits <- d |> count(site_id, name = "visits")

c(rows = nrow(d),
  sites = nrow(visits),
  median_visits = median(visits$visits),
  most_visits = max(visits$visits))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-sites
#| fig-cap: "Left: how many visits each of the 158 sites received: most have three to five, one has thirteen. Right: abundance at the twenty most-visited sites, ordered by site mean. Some sites are consistently empty and some consistently productive, which is what makes repeat visits worth less than independent stations."
#| fig-alt: "Two panels. The left is a bar chart of visits per site, with counts from one to thirteen on the horizontal axis; the tallest bars are at four and five visits, with a long thin tail out to thirteen. The right panel is a strip plot of abundance for twenty sites arranged on the vertical axis in order of their mean, each site shown as a row of points. The lowest rows have all their points at or near zero; the highest rows have points scattered between two and twenty-five. The spread within a row is wide, but the rows clearly differ from one another."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
p1 <- ggplot(visits, aes(visits)) +
  geom_bar(fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:13) +
  labs(x = "Visits to a site", y = "Sites",
       title = "Repeat visits, not fresh stations")

top_sites <- visits |> slice_max(visits, n = 20) |> pull(site_id)

p2 <- d |>
  filter(site_id %in% top_sites) |>
  mutate(site_id = fct_reorder(site_id, abundance, .fun = mean)) |>
  ggplot(aes(abundance, site_id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  labs(x = "Abundance (individuals)", y = NULL,
       title = "The twenty most-visited sites") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

p1 + p2
```

```{r}
#| label: icc
group <- factor(d$site_id)
y     <- log1p(d$abundance)

anova_table <- anova(lm(y ~ group))
mean_sq_between <- anova_table$`Mean Sq`[1]
mean_sq_within  <- anova_table$`Mean Sq`[2]

sizes <- table(group)
m_bar <- (sum(sizes) - sum(sizes^2) / sum(sizes)) / (nlevels(group) - 1)

icc <- (mean_sq_between - mean_sq_within) /
  (mean_sq_between + (m_bar - 1) * mean_sq_within)

design_effect <- 1 + (m_bar - 1) * icc

c(ICC = icc,
  `average group size` = m_bar,
  `design effect` = design_effect,
  `effective sample size` = nrow(d) / design_effect) |>
  round(3)
```

### The cost in precision

The damage is to precision, so we compare a model's standard errors two ways: the ordinary ones,
which assume 720 independent visits, and **cluster-robust** ones, which assume only that
different *sites* are independent.

To make the stakes concrete we also add `site_noise`, a random number drawn once per site
and attached to every visit to it. It has nothing to do with abundance, by construction.
It is the kind of variable a site-level covariate would be: bottom type, management zone,
distance to port.

```{r}
#| label: cluster-robust
set.seed(77)
site_level <- tibble(site_id = unique(d$site_id),
                     site_noise = rnorm(n_distinct(d$site_id)))

dd <- left_join(d, site_level, by = "site_id")

fit <- lm(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + site_noise, data = dd)

# Cluster-robust variance: independence between sites, anything within them.
X <- model.matrix(fit)
u <- residuals(fit)
bread <- solve(t(X) %*% X)
meat <- reduce(unique(dd$site_id), \(acc, s) {
  rows <- dd$site_id == s
  score <- t(X[rows, , drop = FALSE]) %*% u[rows]
  acc + tcrossprod(score)
}, .init = matrix(0, ncol(X), ncol(X)))

G <- n_distinct(dd$site_id)
adjust <- (G / (G - 1)) * ((nrow(X) - 1) / (nrow(X) - ncol(X)))
cluster_se <- sqrt(diag(bread %*% meat %*% bread * adjust))

naive <- summary(fit)$coefficients

tibble(
  term            = rownames(naive),
  estimate        = naive[, 1],
  `naive SE`      = naive[, 2],
  `cluster SE`    = cluster_se,
  `SE inflation`  = cluster_se / naive[, 2],
  `naive p`       = naive[, 4],
  `cluster p`     = 2 * pnorm(-abs(naive[, 1] / cluster_se))
) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-se
#| fig-cap: "Naive and cluster-robust standard errors for the same four coefficients, each expressed as a multiple of its naive value. Chlorophyll's honest standard error is 2.77 times the naive one. Depth and temperature move the other way, which is not a mistake; see the text."
#| fig-alt: "A horizontal dot plot with four terms on the vertical axis and standard error inflation factor on the horizontal axis from 0.8 to 3. A dotted vertical reference line marks 1. Chlorophyll sits far to the right at 2.77. Site noise sits at 1.29. Depth and temperature sit just left of the line at 0.93 and 0.87."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
tibble(term = rownames(naive)[-1],
       inflation = (cluster_se / naive[, 2])[-1]) |>
  mutate(term = fct_reorder(term, inflation)) |>
  ggplot(aes(inflation, term)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted") +
  geom_point(size = 3.4, colour = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]) +
  labs(x = "Cluster-robust SE ÷ naive SE", y = NULL,
       title = "What pretending the visits are independent buys you") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

### And the cost to a predictive model

```{r}
#| label: grouped-cv
model <- workflow() |>
  add_recipe(
    recipe(abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 +
             salinity_psu + substrate + season, data = d) |>
      step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors())
  ) |>
  add_model(rand_forest(trees = 400) |> set_engine("ranger") |> set_mode("regression"))

set.seed(601)
random_cv <- fit_resamples(model, vfold_cv(d, v = 10),
                           metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq))
set.seed(601)
grouped_cv <- fit_resamples(model, group_vfold_cv(d, group = site_id, v = 10),
                            metrics = metric_set(rmse, rsq))

bind_rows(
  collect_metrics(random_cv)  |> mutate(scheme = "Random 10-fold"),
  collect_metrics(grouped_cv) |> mutate(scheme = "Grouped by site")
) |>
  select(scheme, .metric, mean, std_err) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 4)))
```

## Rows against observations

**You have fewer observations than rows.** 720 visits to 158 sites, with an ICC of 0.088, give a
design effect of 1.31 and an effective sample size of **549**. A quarter of the dataset is
redundant: not worthless, but not new information either. Any calculation that used 720 where it
should have used 549 is overconfident by about 15% in its standard errors.

**The precision cost is concentrated, not uniform.** Chlorophyll's honest standard error
is **2.77 times** the naive one, moving its *p*-value from effectively zero to 0.002,
which is still a solid result, but a different claim. Meanwhile the fabricated
`site_noise` variable, which cannot matter, goes from *p* = 0.090 to *p* = 0.187: the
naive analysis was on the road to calling a random number marginally significant.

Depth and temperature go the other way, their standard errors *shrinking* by 7% and 13%. This is
real, not a numerical artefact. Clustering inflates a coefficient's standard error when that
predictor's errors line up within a site, and can shrink it when they do not. The lesson is that
you cannot guess which coefficients are affected or by how much; you have to compute it.

**The predictive cost is much smaller than the inferential one.** Random 10-fold
cross-validation gives RMSE 4.46; grouping the folds by site gives 4.55. That gap is real
but modest, and it is smaller than it would be if sites were tightly packed, because these
158 sites are spread across the whole shelf so a held-out site still has training stations
nearby.

That last clause is important, and it is a warning rather than a reassurance.
[Grouping by site](../07-validation/index.qmd) fixes repeat visits; it does **not** fix the fact
that a held-out site has neighbours in the training set. That is a separate violation, with a
bigger effect, and it is
[two pages away](spatial-and-temporal-dependence.qmd).

::: {.callout-important}
The phrase "we had 720 samples" is the single most common overstatement in survey-based
analysis. Report both numbers: how many observations and how many independent units. If a
reviewer cannot tell from your methods section whether your 720 rows came from 720 places
or 158, the methods section is incomplete.
:::

## Limits of cluster-robust errors

**Cluster-robust standard errors need enough clusters.** The rule of thumb is around 40;
with 158 sites we are comfortable. With eight transects or five vessels, cluster-robust
standard errors are themselves unreliable and a mixed model or a permutation test is the
better route.

**They fix the standard errors, not the estimates.** If sites differ systematically in
ways correlated with your predictors, if the deep sites are also the muddy ones and were
visited more often, the coefficient itself is affected, and a robust standard error around
a biased estimate is a precise answer to the wrong question. A mixed model with a site
random effect, or including site-level means as covariates, addresses that; this page does
not.

**Grouping is only as good as the grouping variable.** `site_id` was recoverable here
because the raw export carried it. Real datasets frequently lose it, when the grab
identifier is dropped in a summary table or the haul is aggregated away, and once it is
gone the dependence is invisible and uncorrectable. Keep the identifier of the unit you
sampled, at every stage of processing.

**Independence is not the only assumption.** A model can have perfectly independent observations
and still be wrong about linearity, about the distribution, or about the range it is being asked
to predict over. Those are the next three pages.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Key points

- Models assume one row is one independent piece of evidence. Repeat visits, sub-samples, and
  profile points are not.
- The **design effect** converts rows into effective observations. Here 720 visits to 158 sites,
  ICC 0.088, gave an effective sample size of **549**.
- Pseudo-replication mainly damages **precision**, not estimates. Chlorophyll's honest standard
  error was 2.77 times the naive one, and a fabricated site-level variable went from *p* = 0.09 to
  *p* = 0.19.
- It is not uniform: two of the four coefficients had *smaller* cluster-robust standard errors.
  Compute it rather than assuming a direction.
- Grouped cross-validation cost only 0.09 RMSE here, because the sites are spread out. It fixes
  repeat visits, not spatial proximity.

:::

## Try it yourself

1. Compute the ICC on `present` instead of `log1p(abundance)`. Is a site's tendency to hold the
   species at all more or less consistent than how many it holds, and which is the more useful
   thing to know about a monitoring site?
2. Restrict the data to sites with at least five visits and recompute the design effect. It will
   rise. Explain why that does *not* mean you should visit fewer sites more often.
